title: HABEaS WebGIS - Hotspot Areas for Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services
text:
What is it?
From 2011 to 2022, I coordinated the HABEaS Project (Hotspot Areas for Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services) which is a free online geographic information system that provides free access to data on biodiversity and ecosystem services in Portugal. The platform enables landowners, NGOs, forest managers, and environmental agencies to access key information on protected areas, endangered and endemic species, rare habitats, carbon storage, erosion risk, and aquifer recharge zones.
 Figure 1 - Distribution of threatened mammals in HABEaS.
Impact
HABEaS WebGIS played a critical role in WWF Portugal’s Green Heart of Cork (GHoC), a landscape initiative to conserve the world’s largest continuous cork-oak woodland across the Tejo & Sado basins (≈500,000 ha), which also overlies the Iberian Peninsula’s largest aquifer (T3). The platform was used to identify biodiversity and ecosystem-service “hotspots” and to target conservation actions where they would have the greatest impact.
GHoC operates through a Payments for Ecosystem Services (PES) scheme in which companies financially reward landowners who practice Forest Stewardship Council (FSC) certified sustainable forest management in those hotspot areas. WWF used HABEaS WebGIS to pinpoint priority sites and then brokered agreements between buyers and landholders—among the sponsors were Coca-Cola Portugal (Refrige), Jerónimo Martins, and Onyria. Between 2011 and 2021, these PES agreements amounted to €79,000.

title: Filipe Dias
text:
Researcher & Consulting Data Analyst – My research examines how management practices and climate change affect Mediterranean oak woodlands, producing peer‑reviewed publications that guide regional and national conservation strategies. In parallel, I collaborate with NGOs and select private firms to develop data‑driven solutions for conservation and land‑use planning.
Currently working at Centro de Estudos Florestais as a Researcher on the project Satellite Information for Resilience Monitoring and Early warning of Ecosystem tipping points (SIRENE), funded by the European Space Agency (ESA), which has the overarching goal of improving the detection and prediction of climate‑driven tipping points in terrestrial ecosystems, especially in vulnerable regions such as tropical rainforests, boreal forests, and drylands.

title: Identification of Priority Areas for Ecological Restoration in Portugal
text:
I was part of a team hired by WWF Portugal to identify priority areas for ecological restoration in mainland Portugal in support of the Re-Store Portugal initiative.




Built a comprehensive geospatial database spanning habitats, species, environmental pressures, and socio-economic factors.
Applied multi-criteria analysis combining ecological, socio-economic, legal, and strategic indicators.
Screened dozens of candidate areas across terrestrial, freshwater, and marine systems, prioritizing those with the highest conservation value and feasibility.
Produced project fiches for each selected area with conservation attributes, key pressures, recommended interventions, and indicative restoration budgets.




We identified nine priority areas across land, sea, and freshwater. These include critical habitats such as coastal wetlands, seagrass meadows, rivers, lagoons, and native forests, all facing significant pressure.
👉 Read the executive summary (PDF)



This work provides a replicable model for prioritizing restoration in Portugal. The approach equips WWF Portugal to mobilize partners, secure funding, and guide implementation of actions that deliver measurable ecological and social benefits.
WWF Portugal plans to invest €1.8 million by 2030 in three of the selected areas: Parque Nacional da Peneda-Gerês, Serra do Caldeirão, and Estuário do Tejo.
